title: Implied Reader, Reflected Text
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Underwood argues that high teacher control in the writing classroom, where the teacher sets the topic, audience and organisation in advance, turns writing into mechanical drudgery with no real reader. Using a lemon-description assignment as an example, he shows how pre-identified problems and given solutions leave the writer with nothing to decide. He contrasts this with writers in the real world, from magazine freelancing to inmates in his prison composition classes, whose purposes and implied readers shape the text. Drawing on Piaget's intensional and extensional schemas and long-term working memory, he explains how writers assess what a reader knows and design text accordingly. His conclusion is that portfolio pedagogy, with shared decision-making and public criteria, is the way to teach writing as problem-solving for a real audience.
points: High teacher control over writing decisions risks mechanising writing and leaving learners bored, stuck or disengaged.
Writing is best learned as problem-solving, which needs experience identifying writer problems and reflecting on decisions with peers and teachers.
Real-world writers are controlled by their implied readers, while school writers are controlled by teachers, so assigned audiences are often token ones.
Piaget's schemas and long-term working memory help explain how writers judge what knowledge a reader has and what the text must elaborate.
Portfolio pedagogy is offered as the central mechanism for sharing control with learners.
quotes: Pedagogy premised on high teacher control, especially in composition pedagogy, risks mechanizing and routinizing writing in meaningless drudgery or production of superficial piffle. Too many learners who might otherwise blossom resist because they are bored with writing the same paragraph about their best friend or their career goals, many struggle without resolution to problems like having nothing to say and not knowing how to say it, many reject serious engagement outright because they are not seriously being engaged.

Such a view underscores a need for a pedagogy of structured protocols and accountability mechanisms (publication deadlines) with visible and public criteria for good writing negotiated by the community.
All you need are words to fill slots in syntax. They don’t have to mean anything.

Writers still instruct their readers in how to read their texts. Ideologically idiotic audiences are more common, probably because of the affordances of technology. But writers in the real world are controlled in varying degrees by their implied reader reflected in their texts. Writers in schools are controlled by teachers.
I got the latter in the composition classes. Their purposes for writing overrode my authority to control their decisions as writers.

If writing is done habitually ignoring the audience, if getting words into sentences in unified paragraphs drives the work, if meaning takes a back seat to form, humanity may be better off turning over writing tasks to chatGPT where meaning is at least the goal of cognition, artificial or organic. As in reading, writing is a whole body, whole brain, whole language, whole culture experience.
